Trying to Conceive

After sex when trying to conceive: routines, hygiene and timing

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

It is understandable to wonder whether something you do after sex could help or harm your chances of pregnancy. There is no required position or timed resting ritual. Focus on comfortable, consensual sex, useful information about the fertile window and care for your health rather than trying to keep every drop of semen inside.

Timing matters more than an after-sex ritual

Conception requires an egg and sperm to meet. The practical fertile window is the five days before ovulation and the day of ovulation, with good chances in the days just before release. That is a window for planning, not a guarantee of pregnancy or proof of safe days for contraception.

Ovulation does not always happen on day 14, even with fairly regular periods. A calendar or test can help estimate timing but cannot identify every cycle perfectly. You do not have to locate one exact moment to have useful intercourse; regular sex can cover the uncertain window.

Calendars and cervical mucus

Count a cycle from the first day of a period to the day before the next starts. Subtracting 14 from its length gives only a rough estimate: day 17 in a 31-day cycle is an example, not a confirmed ovulation day. The interval before the next period varies, and irregular cycles make calendar predictions less reliable.

Near ovulation, secretions may become wetter, slippery, clear and stretchy, like egg white. They can help you notice a pattern, but not everyone sees the same change and absence of obvious mucus does not rule out fertility. Increased sexual desire can also occur, but is not a dependable test of ovulation. Seek advice for a concerning change in discharge rather than treating it as a fertility sign.

Temperature, urine tests and ultrasound

Basal body temperature is measured on waking before getting out of bed. A sustained small rise generally follows ovulation, so a chart mainly gives information afterward; it is not a precise advance prediction and can be unreliable. Home urine kits detect an LH rise, sometimes with another hormone, to predict likely ovulation rather than prove that an egg was released. Health conditions or fertility medicines can affect interpretation.

Follow the instructions for your exact kit rather than assuming afternoon is always best. For example, one Advanced Digital product specifies the first urine after the longest sleep, whereas a Digital model allows a consistent daily testing time. Clinician-directed ultrasound can assess follicles and provide information about likely ovulation when indicated, including in some irregular-cycle evaluations. Scans are not a necessary routine purchase for everyone trying to conceive.

How often should you have sex?

Sex every one to two days during the fertile window is a useful option. NHS advice also suggests sex every two to three days throughout the cycle, which can be easier than intensive tracking. Daily sex is not inherently harmful to fertility, and you do not need to avoid it so sperm can “mature” between each encounter.

Choose a frequency that fits both people’s comfort, consent and circumstances. A rigid schedule can add pressure and reduce enjoyment; missing a planned day does not mean the cycle is wasted. If pain, disability, sexual difficulties or practical barriers make intercourse hard, ask for support rather than forcing it. Follow individualized instructions if you are receiving fertility treatment.

Positions and orgasm are not requirements

No sexual position has been shown to improve natural conception. Face-to-face, a partner on top or rear-entry vaginal penetration should be chosen for comfort, not because one has been proved to direct sperm better. You do not need deeper or painful penetration for a fertility benefit.

Orgasm of the partner receiving vaginal penetration is not required for pregnancy; ejaculation and delivery of sperm are separate processes, and no technique guarantees that conception will occur. Stop activities that hurt and discuss repeated pain or bleeding with a clinician. Urinating, washing or choosing another position is also not contraception and does not prevent sexually transmitted infections.

Do you need to lie still, lift your legs or use a pillow?

You may rest if it feels pleasant, but there is no evidence-based requirement to lie still for 15 minutes after sex. Sperm can enter the cervix quickly; the visible fluid that leaks afterward does not tell you how many sperm have moved onward or whether the encounter can result in pregnancy. Standing or walking does not mean that all sperm have been lost.

Raising your legs or placing a pillow under your hips has no proven fertility advantage. There is no need to hold an uncomfortable pose or blame yourself for getting up. This advice concerns natural conception through intercourse; after a clinical procedure, follow the treating team’s specific instructions.

You can urinate after sex

Urine leaves through the urethra, a different opening from the vagina, so urinating does not wash sperm out of the vagina or reduce the chance of conception. There is no need to wait 15 minutes before going to the toilet. Do not hold urine when you need to go.

NHS UTI-prevention advice recommends urinating soon after sex and gentle cleaning of the surrounding skin. These measures may help but do not guarantee freedom from infection. Recurrent burning or urgency needs assessment; possible pregnancy with urinary symptoms, fever, chills, flank pain or blood in urine needs urgent advice. Do not rely on repeated washing or urination to treat an infection.

Showering and gentle hygiene

You can shower after intercourse; washing the outside does not flush out sperm that have entered the reproductive tract. Clean the external genital skin gently with water, avoid scented products and dry without scrubbing. There is no fertility requirement to delay washing or to leave semen on the skin.

Do not douche or wash inside the vagina with soap, water jets or other products. Internal washing can irritate tissue and disturb the vaginal environment; it is neither fertility treatment nor pregnancy or STI prevention. If symptoms follow sex, choose assessment rather than stronger cleaning. Hygiene is care for comfort and health, not a test of whether you deserve a pregnancy.

Massage, relaxation and emotional support

Gentle massage, rest, meditation or comfortable yoga may help you relax or feel supported. They are not proven after-sex methods of making sperm meet the egg or guaranteeing pregnancy. Difficulty conceiving is not evidence that you failed to relax enough.

If receiving fertility treatment or if pregnancy is possible, check complementary therapies and products with your clinician; some herbs or supplements can interact with medicines or be unsuitable. HFEA notes that stress has not been conclusively shown to worsen fertility-treatment outcomes; that statement is about treatment studies, not proof that every stress-reduction method boosts natural conception. Seek emotional or relationship support when you want it.

Useful preparation and when to ask for help

Review medicines and health conditions before pregnancy and do not stop prescriptions on your own. NHS advice recommends 400 micrograms of folic acid daily when trying and through the first 12 weeks; some risks need a clinician-prescribed higher dose. Avoid smoking and alcohol when planning pregnancy, and discuss help if needed. These steps support health rather than promise immediate conception.

ASRM suggests fertility evaluation after 12 months of trying under age 35, six months from 35, and sooner over 40 or with known risks such as irregular or absent periods, suspected endometriosis or a sperm concern. Relevant partners should be assessed. Test for pregnancy from a missed period, or at least 21 days after the last unprotected sex if you do not know when the period is due. Repeat an early negative if pregnancy remains possible. If pregnancy is possible, new one-sided lower abdominal or pelvic pain or unusual bleeding needs urgent same-day assessment even without a positive test. Shoulder-tip pain with possible pregnancy needs immediate medical advice even without abdominal pain. In a known pregnancy, contact maternity care immediately for any vaginal bleeding, even light spotting. Severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, fainting or loss of consciousness, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or heavy vaginal bleeding require emergency care now. Pregnancy with bleeding and shoulder pain, marked dizziness or faintness also needs emergency care. Do not drive yourself.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Choose comfortable, consensual vaginal intercourse regularly rather than a compulsory position or after-sex ritual. Tracking can estimate the fertile window but cannot guarantee pregnancy; follow your exact ovulation-kit instructions.

Urinate when you need to and wash the outside gently. Avoid vaginal douching, painful activities and unreviewed fertility remedies; ask for assessment of persistent pain, bleeding or urinary symptoms.

Review medicines and folic acid before pregnancy, and arrange fertility assessment according to age and known risks. Ask for support if trying to conceive causes distress; relaxation is for wellbeing, not a requirement for deserving pregnancy.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record cycles, symptoms, test instructions and questions for care. It cannot confirm ovulation or pregnancy, diagnose infertility or infection, prescribe a fertility ritual or replace clinical assessment and emergency care.

When to seek help

Do not force painful sex, delay needed urination, douche or start unreviewed fertility remedies. If pregnancy is possible, new one-sided lower abdominal or pelvic pain or unusual bleeding needs urgent same-day assessment even without a positive test. Shoulder-tip pain with possible pregnancy needs immediate medical advice even without abdominal pain. In a known pregnancy, contact maternity care immediately for any vaginal bleeding, even light spotting. Severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, fainting or loss of consciousness, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or heavy vaginal bleeding require emergency care now. Pregnancy with bleeding and shoulder pain, marked dizziness or faintness also needs emergency care. Do not drive yourself. Urinary symptoms with possible pregnancy, fever, chills, flank pain or blood in urine need urgent medical advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • No post-sex position, pillow, leg raising or 15-minute rest is required to improve natural conception.
  • Urinating or showering after sex does not wash sperm out of the reproductive tract; do not delay needed urination.
  • Use gentle external hygiene and avoid internal vaginal washing or douching.
  • Fertile-window estimates and regular comfortable intercourse are more useful than a rigid ritual; daily sex is not inherently harmful.
  • Relaxation can support wellbeing without guaranteeing pregnancy; seek age- and risk-appropriate fertility care.

Frequently asked questions

How can I estimate ovulation?

Cycle records, changes in slippery cervical mucus and urine LH tests can help estimate timing, but are not perfect proof of ovulation. Temperature rises usually give information afterward. Follow your exact kit’s timing instructions; ultrasound is selected by a clinician when appropriate.

How often should we have sex?

Every one to two days in the fertile window is one option; every two to three days through the cycle is another practical approach. Daily sex does not inherently damage fertility. Choose a consensual, comfortable frequency rather than forcing a rigid schedule.

Which position is best for pregnancy?

None has been shown to improve natural conception. Choose a comfortable position and avoid painful penetration. Orgasm of the partner receiving vaginal penetration, raised legs or a pillow are not requirements and do not guarantee pregnancy.

Does massage after sex increase the chance?

It may feel relaxing, but it is not a proven conception method. Enjoy safe comfort measures if you wish; do not blame stress or buy therapies on the promise of pregnancy. Ask your clinician about safety during treatment or possible pregnancy.

Must I wait 15 minutes before standing or urinating?

No. There is no required 15-minute rest for natural conception. Urine leaves through a separate opening and does not remove vaginal sperm. Go when you need to; urinating soon after sex is part of NHS UTI-prevention advice but is not an infection guarantee.

Does semen leaking out mean the chance is lost?

No. Leakage is common and does not show whether sperm have entered the cervix or whether conception will occur. You do not need to keep every drop inside, lift your legs or stay uncomfortable.

Can I shower or clean inside the vagina?

You can shower and gently clean the outside with water. Do not douche or wash internally: it can irritate and disrupt the vaginal environment. Neither washing nor urinating prevents pregnancy or STIs.

When should I seek medical help?

Use age- and risk-appropriate fertility evaluation, and ask earlier for irregular periods, known risks or painful sex. Urinary symptoms with possible pregnancy, fever, flank pain or blood need urgent advice. If pregnancy is possible, new one-sided lower abdominal or pelvic pain or unusual bleeding needs urgent same-day assessment even without a positive test. Shoulder-tip pain with possible pregnancy needs immediate medical advice even without abdominal pain. In a known pregnancy, contact maternity care immediately for any vaginal bleeding, even light spotting. Severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, fainting or loss of consciousness, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or heavy vaginal bleeding require emergency care now. Pregnancy with bleeding and shoulder pain, marked dizziness or faintness also needs emergency care. Do not drive yourself.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
